entries.title: Trump’s Anti-Fraud Crusade Casts a Long Shadow Over Minnesota Governor’s Race
entries.summary: Whoever controls the governor’s mansion next year will contend with fallout from the White House’s large withdrawal of federal Medicaid funding earlier this year.
entries.content:
Republicans have made Minnesota central to their crusade against fraud in federal government programs. Now, both gubernatorial candidates are arguing they’re better equipped to right the ship.

The stakes are high for Minnesota’s federal programs: The White House is currently withholding close to $200 million in federal Medicaid payments over fraud concerns in Minnesota’s public health programs, and Trump has accused outgoing Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat, of allowing the state to become a “hub of fraudulent money laundering activity.” The state’s large Somali population also faced an intense immigration crackdown operation last winter, with officials in part citing allegations of fraud in public programs.

Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar on Tuesday tried to make an early entry in the lane Republicans have dominated for the last year as voters turn to the general election. Her first general election TV ad promises “a top-to-bottom audit of state government” to rid the state of “the waste and the fraud and the abuse” — a phrase that’s typically been used by conservatives, including the Trump officials who have rescinded the state’s federal funding.

“She knows it's a massive issue,” Amy Frederiksen, a Republican strategist and former state Senate majority leader, told NOTUS. Frederiksen says Democrats across the country haven’t been as vocal about combatting fraud, but “sometimes there's just local issues that rise up that even obscure some of the national pressures.”

Republican nominee Lisa Demuth — who has made fighting fraud a legislative priority during her time as state House speaker — says she’ll implement an updated anti-fraud plan during her first 90 days as governor. She also proposes firing all existing commissioners and replacing them with experts who are “committed to ending the culture of fraud,” restructuring state program eligibility requirements and establishing an independent state inspector general’s office.

Throughout her campaign, Demuth has tied Klobuchar to Walz, saying the senator’s tenure would be like a “Walz third term.” The governor dropped his bid for another term amid ongoing criticism for his administration’s handling of fraud in Minnesota’s state programs, and did not endorse Klobuchar in the primaries.

“By finally cleaning up the fraud and working with the federal government, I will be able to lift the federal freeze that’s been impacting the legitimate providers harmed by the failed leadership of Tim Walz and Amy Klobuchar,” Demuth said during a Tuesday news conference.

Demuth is likely to keep trying to tie her opponent to Walz, Frederiksen said — but the link might not resonate with voters because she “wasn't overseeing programs and these departments” while serving the state in D.C.

As a senator, Klobuchar says she successfully pushed for more prosecutors to handle cases related to the Feeding Our Future scandal, in which a child-nutrition program submitted fraudulent records to secure more than $240 million in federal funds.

“While others were just talking about fraud — I took action,” she wrote in a Tuesday post on X.

Last December, conservative YouTuber Nick Shirley posted a viral video alleging sweeping fraud at daycare centers run by the Somali community in Minnesota, and the state saw a surge in federal law enforcement presence soon after. Demuth said Minnesota’s Republican caucus had worked directly with Shirley and agency whistleblowers “to get the information out to the public and to hold the Walz administration accountable.”

Fraud has since become an increasingly salient issue for state voters, with 81% of respondents saying they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned about the level of fraud in state social services programs in a June poll. The same poll showed 45% of likely voters trusted Republicans to combat fraud, while 38% picked Democrats.

While Klobuchar had maintained a close friendship with Walz for years — including introducing the then-vice presidential candidate at the 2024 DNC — she began to distance herself as the governor’s political profile soured. Throughout her gubernatorial campaign, Klobuchar has contrasted their records to defy Republicans’ attempts to tie her to Walz’s fraud troubles.

“You are right to be angry about the fraud. It is unacceptable and it must end. It should never have happened to begin with,” Klobuchar said at a May news conference announcing her anti-fraud plan.

As governor, Klobuchar says she’ll establish a state “Do Not Pay” database to automatically block entities convicted of fraud from accessing grants or contracts, conduct unannounced inspections of groups receiving funds and modernize state technology systems. She also supports creating an inspector general’s office to coordinate across agencies.

Frederiksen thinks speaking out against fraud is “a message that works dually” for both parties. Fighting fraud involves both Republicans’ desire to protect taxpayer money and Democrats’ priority of safeguarding federal assistance programs, she said.

“I just don't understand why the Democrats haven't been more vocal on it, and I think that Senator Klobuchar must feel the same because I think the message works on a lot of levels,” Frederiksen said. “It's certainly not just a GOP message, or shouldn't be, but it has been.”

entries.title: Local Media Mogul Beats Trump’s Pick in Crowded Florida House Race
entries.summary: The Florida race included two former members of Congress hoping to rehabilitate their political careers.
entries.content:
Jim Schwartzel was projected to win the Republican primary for Florida’s 19th Congressional District, prevailing in a crowded race for Rep. Byron Donalds’ open seat, which he opted to vacate in order to mount a run for governor.

The Associated Press called the race Tuesday for Schwartzel, a conservative local media mogul, who bested nearly a dozen candidates — including President Donald Trump’s pick, Catalina Lauf, and two former members of Congress with controversial tenures.

As the Republican nominee, Schwartzel will face Democrat Victor Arias in November. Schwartzel is likely to become the next representative for the district rated “Solid R” by the Cook Political Report.

Schwartzel spent nearly $1.9 million through July 29, according to Federal Elections Commission totals. He had raised concerns about his opponents’ lack of local ties to southwest Florida, leaning heavily on his status as one of the few candidates who is a lifelong resident of the state.

Lauf, a former Commerce Department adviser during Trump’s first term, earned the second-highest vote share after spending just $1.6 million on her campaign. She received a last-minute endorsement from Trump on Aug. 13, and earned the support of Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna.

Lauf faced criticism for recently moving to Florida from her home state of Illinois, where she ran for Congress in 2022. Her lack of ties to the district became a scandal of sorts in the waning days of the primary campaign after an audio clip showed Lauf struggling to answer questions about local officials in her newly adopted city of Bonita Springs.

Many of the frontrunners’ foes previously held elected positions in other states, before recently moving to Florida.

Former Illinois state Sen. Jim Oberweis had the largest war chest in the race with $5.3 million, nearly all of which came from a personal loan to the campaign.

Former New York Rep. Chris Collins, whom Trump pardoned in 2020 after he served two months of his 26-month sentence for insider trading and lying to the FBI, was also in the running. He spent more than $2.4 million of his entirely self-funded campaign of $3.4 million.

Former Rep. Madison Cawthorn, who served one term in Congress for North Carolina before losing his reelection bid in 2023, also moved to the district to run for the seat. The House Ethics Committee had admonished Cawthorn over accusations that he improperly promoted cryptocurrency just before he lost reelection to Congress. He had also faced sexual misconduct allegations from his past and legal troubles for bringing a loaded gun to an airport, as well as ticketed for excessive speeding and charged with driving on a revoked license.

Cawthorn loaned $800,000 to his campaign, which spent more than $720,000 on the race.

Other candidates included former congressional staffer Ola Hawatmeh, pardoned Jan. 6 rioter John Strand, businessman Greg “Tex” Burkowski, Marine Corps veteran Mike Pedersen and nurse Linda Sawyer.

This story has been updated with the race call for the Democratic nominee.

entries.title: Cory Mills Loses Primary as He Faces Investigations Into His Behavior
entries.summary: The Florida Republican’s defeat ends a career in Congress defined by controversy.
entries.content:
Embattled Rep. Cory Mills of Florida was projected to lose his reelection bid to a former local television news host amid a growing list of scandals and investigations that affected his standing within the House Republican Conference.

The Associated Press called the race Tuesday for Ryan Elijah, who had the backing of some members of the Florida congressional delegation and handily outraised the Mills in recent months.

The two-term congressman’s defeat ends a career in Congress that was defined by controversy. Mills is currently under criminal investigation by the Justice Department, which is looking into his personal and campaign finances, a source familiar told NOTUS.

He is also under investigation by the House Ethics Committee for a range of allegations, including domestic violence against his partner in his Washington, D.C., apartment, campaign-finance violations and accusations that his company held government contracts while he was a sitting member of Congress.

Mills has remained defiant and denied the allegations and has said he has no knowledge of a DOJ investigation into him.

On top of these investigations, Mills has run into other issues throughout his years in Congress.

NOTUS first reported in 2025 about uncertainties surrounding Mills’ military service record. Five people who served with Mills in Iraq — including two men Mills is credited with saving on official military documents — said they have no recollection of Mills being involved in the incidents.

NOTUS also reported last year that Mills was caught with sex workers while on a rescue mission in Tbilisi, Georgia, in 2021 when he was a congressional candidate. He appeared to travel on to Afghanistan separate from the rest of the group, who were enraged by Mills’ behavior given the sensitive nature of the mission, sources told NOTUS.

The controversy surrounding Mills got so intense that even some of his own Republican colleagues sought to expel him from Congress. Some members of the Florida delegation, led by Rep. Mike Haridopolos, endorsed Elijah over him.

Mills also struggled to raise money — he brought in only $59,000 in the second quarter of the year, according to Federal Election Commission numbers, and only had $81,000 on hand.
entries.author: Reese Gorman

entries.title: The Anti-Abortion Movement Is Split Over Sen. Darline Graham
entries.summary: One anti-abortion leader told NOTUS she has “real concerns” that Graham will not be “a pro-life fighter.”
entries.content:
Sen. Darline Graham’s lack of legislative record is threatening her chances in the South Carolina Senate Republican runoff, specifically on an issue that her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, dominated: ending abortion.

“One of the lessons that’s been very clear to pro-life activists and really conservative party activists over the last few months in the U.S. Senate is we need people who have got our backs and are true believers and are going to get things done and advance our agenda,” Kristan Hawkins, president of the prominent anti-abortion group Students for Life Action, told NOTUS.

But, Hawkins added, she has “real concerns about if [Graham is] really going to be a pro-life fighter in Washington, D.C.”

SFLA endorsed Rep. Ralph Norman in the runoff, citing his track record introducing and supporting anti-abortion legislation in the House and his involvement in supporting a lawsuit to defund Planned Parenthood. Hawkins’ group, which was the first national anti-abortion group to weigh in on the race, said Norman signed its candidate pledge committing to back anti-abortion priorities.

The organization reached out to Graham multiple times while it was deciding which candidate to endorse but received no response.

“We have not heard back from her team. Apparently, she thinks she’s got bigger fish to fry,” Hawkins said.

The endorsement was a blow for Graham, whose standing as a relatively unknown senator has led to a divide within the Republican Party over who to support in the runoff, even with President Donald Trump backing her. She was appointed to the Senate last month after the sudden death of her brother, who was viewed as a reliable anti-abortion vote over his three decades in Congress.

“Lindsey Graham fought for life, and he fought to see the end of abortion,” Hawkins said. “I don’t think the torch has been passed.”

Darline Graham received 33% of the vote in the special Republican primary earlier this month, the most votes among Republicans in the race. However, since she failed to get a majority of the votes, Graham and Norman, who received 25%, will face off in a runoff election next Tuesday.

Now, a rift in the anti-abortion movement is playing out over who its best advocate is.

Just a day after SFLA announced its endorsement, a decision that Hawkins said she knew would be seen as “controversial,” another major anti-abortion group, Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, backed Graham.

“I used to know Sen. Darline Graham through her brother, the great Senate pro-life champion and my good friend, Sen. Lindsey Graham. But now, I’ve gotten to know her directly for who she is. Her pro-life values are passionate and deeply rooted in principle,” Marjorie Dannenfelser, SBA’s president, said in a statement. “I urge all South Carolinians to vote for her.”

In a press release touting the support, Graham said she was “proud to be the most pro-life candidate in this race.” She bragged about the support in Tuesday’s debate against Norman, saying she was “honored and excited” to be backed by the group.

SBA’s endorsement was not surprising. The organization had a close relationship with Lindsey Graham and had already committed to deploying its grassroots to South Carolina as part of its $80 million planned spending this election cycle.

Hawkins said that last week she spoke to staff from the National Right to Life Committee, another big anti-abortion group that often gets involved in political races, and told them about Graham’s donation to Shealy. The NRLC told NOTUS that it planned to endorse in the race, but it did not reveal which candidate it would be backing nor say when it would be announced.

But previous donations tie Graham to abortion rights supporters.

She accepted a $10,000 donation from Denali Leadership PAC, a leadership PAC affiliated with Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), one of only two Republican senators who support abortion rights. In 2020, Graham donated $100 to former Republican South Carolina state Sen. Katrina Shealy, who gained national attention in 2022 when she played a key role in blocking a near-total abortion ban from becoming law in the state.

The Daily Beast, which was the first to report the Shealy donation, said that shortly after the outlet reached out to Graham’s campaign for comment on the story, her office posted on X that the senator was “proud to be pro-life and to stand up for the unborn” and endorsed seven anti-abortion bills in the Senate.

None of the bills she endorsed are abortion bans.

When asked about the post, Hawkins told NOTUS that Graham “didn’t support the Life at Conception Act,” a bill that would grant embryos personhood rights, effectively outlawing abortion. Hawkins added that SFLA had reached out to Graham about potentially having her be the lead Senate sponsor for the “Clean Water for All Life Act,” a bill which would restrict access to abortion pills and has been introduced in the House.

Graham’s campaign declined to respond to NOTUS’ detailed questions, including what her stances on abortion are and whether she agreed with Shealy. The former state senator told The New York Times that she and Graham are close friends but never spoke about politics, but Graham told reporters on Monday that they were not friends and said she was “definitely pro-life.”

The criticism over her record has seemingly gotten to Graham’s campaign.

On Tuesday afternoon, Graham spokesperson Abby Zilch posted on X that Norman had donated $1,000 to former Democratic South Carolina state Rep. Leon Stavrinakis. In 2022, he voted against a six-week abortion ban in the state.

But Zilch did not mention that the donation was from 2015, when Stavrinakis was running for Charleston mayor in a nonpartisan election against another Democrat, John Tecklenburg. Tecklenburg, who was backed by progressives, ultimately won that race.

Norman and his campaign did not respond to NOTUS’ requests for comment over text and email.
entries.author: Oriana González

entries.title: What to Do In the D.C. Area This Weekend (Aug. 21)
entries.summary: The National Book Festival, Improvapolozza and the return of live music at the Carter Barron Amphitheater.
entries.content:
Thursday 


Washington Improv Theater’s Improvapolooza 2026 
Studio Theatre, 1501 14th St. NW, 7:30 p.m., $25 for a nightly pass 

Thursday marks Day 2 of this five-day festival, which features hundreds of local improv pros and amateurs (many of them federal employees) aiming to entertain, as long as you supply a country, a favorite food and the name of your ex-boyfriend. Thursday’s lineup includes a cast of former athletes, several vampire-themed sessions and a sketch entirely sung a cappella.

JazzDC AllStars at Carter Barron Amphitheater
4850 Colorado Ave. NW, 6 p.m., $15

For 10 years, Rock Creek Park’s Carter Barron Amphitheater has lain fallow like a cursed castle in a modern fairytale, surrounded by chain-link fence and overgrown with plants. That all changes this weekend, when live music returns to the venue for the first time since 2016. The Rock Creek Conservancy, D.C. Jazz Festival and Washington Performing Arts teamed up to revive the amphitheater with a trio of shows. Sunday’s show is already sold out, but tickets remain for the JazzDC Allstars on Thursday and Sylver Logan Sharp and the Groovement ALLstars on Friday.

More to explore: “Wine and Design” origami night at the Smithsonian’s National Postal Museum

Friday 


Ledisi: For Dinah at Strathmore
5301 Tuckerman Lane, North Bethesda, 8 p.m., $29 to $139 

The versatile vocalist Ledisi has portrayed gospel legend Mahalia Jackson twice in films and received a Grammy nomination for covering songs made famous by Nina Simone. Now she’s honoring jazz chanteuse Dinah Washington, and touring in support of her 2025 album, “For Dinah.” Produced by “Jazz Night in America” host Christian McBride, this album of sultry night music includes standards like “Caravan,” “What a Difference a Day Makes” and “This Bitter Earth.” She will be performing at Strathmore on Friday and Saturday.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“Michael” screening at Films at the Stone
1964 Independence Ave. SW, 8 p.m., free

Outdoor movie season continues this weekend as “Michael” screens at the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial on Friday night. The Michael Jackson biopic released this year focuses mostly on the singer’s musical milestones, and there’s no more thrilling way to see the film than projected onto the memorial’s flat side, along the Tidal Basin.

More to explore: “Beltway Bungalow” vintage fair in Alexandria

Saturday 


National Book Festival 
Washington Convention Center, 801 Allen Y. Lew Place NW, 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., free (tickets required)

This annual celebration of literature is as much about books as it is celebrities with books to promote. This year’s A-list authors include “Wicked” star Cynthia Erivo debuting a memoir; SNL alum Kate McKinnon chatting about her foray into young adult fiction and filmmaker Martin Scorsese talking about — well, there doesn’t seem to be a book involved but there’s always “Taxi Driver.” Don’t take kids to that, but younger readers will enjoy read-aloud events on the Story District stage. For Orioles fans, owner David Rubenstein will sit down with announcer Kevin Brown. But be forewarned: Rubenstein will not be signing copies of his book “Inside the Owner’s Box,” probably because he doesn’t want to hear your thoughts on the Adley Rutschman trade.

Richard O’Brien’s “The Rocky Horror Show” 
Monumental Theatre Company at Dance Place, 3225 8th St. NE, 8 p.m. $45

You’ve seen the movie — maybe you’re even sung along at one of those late-night screenings — but have you ever seen “Rocky Horror Show” live? Now’s your chance, especially if the current Broadway run is beyond your budget. Monumental Theatre Company’s marquee event is its annual summer musical, and this year it’s offering a cult classic staged as an immersive cabaret. The Brookland venue Dance Place remains transformed into Dr. Frank-N-Furter's laboratory through Sept. 6.

More to explore: “Summer Saturdays” at George Mason’s Gunston Hall

Sunday 


“The Notebook” at The National Theatre
1321 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m., $81 to $223

May we suggest taking Mom to brunch, then to The National Theatre for a Sunday matinee performance of “The Notebook”? The mid-aughts indie pop ingénue Ingrid Michaelson adapted the 2004 film, which was already an adaptation of the Nicholas Sparks novel, into a Broadway musical that drew mixed reviews. “What makes you sigh and weep may leave the person next to you bored and stony,” opined New York Times critic Jesse Green. The tour runs at The National through Aug. 30. Grab the tissues (just in case) and see if watching lovers embrace as the rain falls onstage turns on the waterworks for you (or your mom).

“A Very Laufey Day”
Candlelight concerts at National City Christian Church, 5 Thomas Circle NW, 6:45 and 8:45 p.m., $52 to $105

The Icelandic singer Laufey is not performing Sunday at National City Christian Church (which also functions as a rental venue), but the former DMV resident did personally curate this tribute performance. Surrounded by onstage candles, the Listeo String Quartet will perform 21st century torch songs including “Dreamer,” “Lover Girl” and “Let You Break My Heart Again.”

More to explore: Perreito and Coffee social at Llamabar
